scenario: The generative track has 8 papers today, 4 with deep dives. Pinterest's PinRec serves the home feed, search and related items with one generative retrieval model, and the key is generating toward the target action. OMG finds that generative recommenders do poorly when few history items share the target's category, and inserts a small iterating network between encoder and decoder that turns behavior-leaning representations into what code generation needs. CoFiRec codes Semantic IDs coarse to fine by category, text and collaborative signal. Another paper distills a sequential model's item distribution into a parallel generative model. Teams doing Semantic ID retrieval can start with PinRec and OMG.

papers.title: PinRec: Unified Generative Retrieval Model for Pinterest Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Edoardo Botta, Jaewon Yang, Yi-Ping Hsu, Laksh Bhasin, Yilin Chen
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval methods employ sequential modeling techniques, like transformers, to generate candidate items for recommender systems. These methods have demonstrated promising results in academic benchmarks, surpassing traditional retrieval models such as two-tower architectures. However, a key limitation is that current approaches require a separate model for each product surface, as building a unified model that accommodates the different business needs of various surfaces has proven challenging. Furthermore, existing methods often fail to capture the evolution of user interests over a sequence, focusing instead on only predicting the next item. This paper introduces Pinrec, a novel unified generative retrieval model for all of Pinterest's recommendation surfaces, including home feed, search, and related pins. Pinrec is pretrained on user activity sequences aggregated across surfaces, then fine-tuned for each surface using that surface's impression data. This pretraining-fine-tuning approach enables a single unified model while still adapting to the needs of individual surfaces. To better align recommendations with surface-specific business goals, Pinrec incorporates a novel outcome-conditioned generation mechanism that targets different outcomes for each surface, which further enhances the impact of fine-tuning. Our experiments show that Pinrec balances performance, diversity, and efficiency, delivering significant gains such as +4% increase in search saves. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first rigorous study of a unified generative retrieval model built and deployed at Pinterest scale, marking a significant milestone in the field.
papers.summary: Recommender systems usually run a separate retrieval model for the home feed, search and related items, because each surface wants something different: saves on the home feed, outbound clicks to buy on search, and continued browsing on related items. This Pinterest KDD 2026 paper replaces all three with one generative retrieval model, PinRec. It is pretrained on site-wide behavior, fine-tuned on each surface's logs, and told at generation time which action to aim for. ==Conditioning on the target action matters far more than unifying the model==. Removing that condition cuts offline recall on the three surfaces by 7.5% to 12.6%. Added to search as one retrieval source online, it raised saves by 3.88%.

papers.title: Unifying Behavior Modeling and Semantic Generation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Binquan Wu, Xinbo Chen, Yicheng Luo, Yuhao Ke, Jingye Li
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) assigns each item content-derived Semantic IDs (SIDs) and employs a sequence-to-sequence model to generate the target item's SIDs based on past user sessions. This paradigm typically outperforms sequential recommendation (SR) methods that rely solely on behavior modeling. However, GR methods suffer from semantic preference bias, where they favor semantically similar items while neglecting items with weak semantic similarity but manifest behavioral relevance--patterns that SR models capture more effectively through behavior modeling. In this work, we propose OMG, a GR method that unifies behavior modeling and semantic generation to produce recommendations that seamlessly integrate both information. First, we introduce Hybrid Behavior-Semantic Encoding, enabling OMG to capture salient user behavioral patterns in addition to semantic correlation when encoding interaction sequences, aiming to recall items with certain behavioral relevance but weak semantic similarity. Then, we propose Behavior-Semantic Latent Reasoning. It iteratively refines the encoder output, progressively transforming it from the behavioral space to the semantic space, and leverages the resulting trajectory to guide SIDs decoding, thereby bridging behavior modeling and semantic generation. Finally, we employ Behavior-Reinforced Semantic Generation, which introduces reinforcement learning with behavior-aware rewards to enhance the model's reasoning capability and better align the decoder's generation process with user behavior. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that OMG consistently outperforms baseline methods.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that write the next item's Semantic ID code by code have a systematic bias. This KDD 2026 paper from South China University of Technology finds that the fewer items in a user's history share the target's category, the worse they do against classic behavior-only sequential models; in the worst group, TIGER's NDCG@10 trails SASRec by 30%. The cause: the encoder learns which item comes next, while the decoder must write its code. OMG inserts a two-layer network between them; each step adds the previous state to the encoder's final state and runs it through the network again. ==Each step predicts both the next item and the first code, with the latter weighted more each step==, and all intermediate states go to the decoder. That one part lifts metrics by 14.5% on average while adding only 0.16% compute.

papers.title: CoFiRec: Coarse-to-Fine Tokenization for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Tianxin Wei, Xuying Ning, Xuxing Chen, Ruizhong Qiu, Yupeng Hou
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation models next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over tokenized user histories, where each item is represented as a sequence of discrete tokens. However, existing methods typically construct these tokens by compressing heterogeneous item attributes, such as ID, category, title, and description, into a single latent representation before quantization, which obscures the hierarchical structure of item semantics and limits their ability to capture how user preferences evolve from broad interests to specific choices during web interactions. To address this issue, we propose CoFiRec, a generative recommendation framework that explicitly incorporates Coarse-to-Fine semantic structure into both item tokenization and decoding. Specifically, CoFiRec organizes item information into multiple semantic levels, spanning high-level categories, fine-grained textual content, and collaborative signals. Building on this design, we introduce the CoFiRec Tokenizer, which tokenizes each semantic level independently while preserving their structural order, thereby better reflecting how users refine their preferences and enabling more structured generation. During autoregressive decoding, the language model generates item tokens progressively from coarse to fine, allowing the recommendation process to better capture the natural refinement of user intent. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks and backbone models demonstrate that CoFiRec consistently outperforms existing baselines, and our theoretical analysis further shows that structured hierarchical tokenization reduces the expected dissimilarity between generated items and ground-truth targets. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/YennNing/CoFiRec.
papers.summary: When shopping online, people usually look at a broad category before picking a specific item. Yet most generative recommenders build Semantic IDs by mashing an item's category, title, description and collaborative signal into one vector before quantizing it, so that coarse-to-fine structure is lost. This UIUC and Meta paper proposes CoFiRec, which ==splits an item into category, text and collaborative levels, codes each separately, and generates them coarse to fine==. Across several public datasets and backbones, it beats the strongest traditional and generative baselines by 7.27% on average in Recall and NDCG. On cold items the gain reaches 10.0%, versus 4.7% on warm items.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yixuan Xu, Hailin Liu, Linxiang Peng, Can Yang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation with semantic IDs represents each item as a sequence of discrete codes derived from its semantic representation and predicts these codes to generate recommendations. Existing semantic-ID recommenders are typically trained with hard labels for the observed next item. Although such supervision identifies the target, it provides no explicit distributional information about alternative items conditioned on the same user history. Sequential recommenders can supply this item-level predictive knowledge, but transferring it to semantic-ID generation is challenging because the teacher and student operate in item and code spaces, respectively. We propose two complementary knowledge-distillation objectives for parallel semantic-ID recommenders, which predict all code positions simultaneously without autoregressive prefix conditioning. Item Distribution Matching (IDM) reconstructs a catalogue-level item distribution from the student's parallel code predictions and aligns it with the teacher's item distribution. Code Marginal Matching (CMM) projects the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position using fixed item-to-code assignments, then matches the resulting code marginals to the corresponding student heads. Both objectives transfer the teacher's soft distributional knowledge while preserving the student's parallel prediction structure. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that both methods consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. On average, IDM improves Recall@10 by 15.39%, while CMM improves NDCG@10 by 8.28%. These results demonstrate that distillation in either reconstructed item space or code-marginal space can substantially strengthen hard-label supervision for parallel generative recommendation.
papers.summary: In generative recommendation with Semantic IDs, training only tells the model which item came next, so it learns nothing about how likely the other items were given the same history. A classic sequential recommender can provide that distribution, but it scores items while the generative model predicts codes position by position, so the knowledge is hard to distill directly. This paper from HKUST and others proposes two distillation objectives for parallel models that predict all code positions at once. One rebuilds a catalogue-wide item distribution from the student's code predictions and aligns it with the teacher; ==the other spreads the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position==. On average, the first lifts Recall@10 by 15.39% and the second lifts NDCG@10 by 8.28%.

papers.title: Separating Thinking from Spelling for Efficient Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Danil Gusak, Anna Volodkevich, Ivan Oseledets, Evgeny Frolov
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders retrieve items by writing their semantic IDs (SIDs) code by code under trie-constrained beam search, an approach now deployed on large web platforms. Standard autoregressive interfaces pay for the SID length K twice: a history of T items enters the backbone as TK code tokens, and every beam-search step runs through the backbone, so returning B candidates costs O(BK) backbone decode tokens per user. The second cost often dominates, and it grows with the backbone, the SID depth and the candidate budget. We introduce Deco (decoding from concepts), which separates reading the history from writing the identifier. The backbone reads each history item as one fused token and condenses the history once into a compact next-item concept; a light KV-cached decoder conditioned on the concept and the generated prefix runs the entire beam search, while the identifiers, the trie and the autoregressive factorization stay unchanged. The decoder approaches full-backbone accuracy with cross-entropy alone, and distillation improves it further. On seven datasets from e-commerce, movies and music streaming, Deco achieves comparable or better accuracy than both a standard generative recommender and the full-backbone teacher with fused inputs, while delivering 3.2--8.6$\times$ their throughput under a 50 ms p95 latency budget in a production-style serving pipeline. Delegating beam search makes larger candidate pools and models practical: Deco generates 1000 candidates faster than its teacher generates 100, and with a 1.5B-parameter LLM backbone, it matches the 69M-parameter teacher's throughput while achieving higher accuracy.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders retrieve by writing an item's Semantic ID code by code, and every beam-search step runs through the large backbone, so the cost grows with more candidates and longer codes. It is often the main expense. This paper proposes Deco, which separates reading the history from writing the code. The backbone reads the history once and condenses it into a vector for the next item, and ==a light cached decoder runs the whole beam search==, with codes and the prefix tree unchanged. On seven e-commerce, movie and music datasets, accuracy matches or beats the original model. Under a 50 ms latency budget, throughput is 3.2 to 8.6 times higher.

papers.title: SAGE: Sequence-level Adaptive Gradient Evolution for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yu Xie, Xing Kai Ren, Ying Qi, Ping Yang, Yao Hu
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders increasingly train Semantic-ID models to autoregressively generate length-L slates, aligned to user feedback by reinforcement learning. Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization (GBPO) stabilizes this stage with a BCE-stable asymmetric gradient bound, but its clipping boundary is computed per sample and is therefore blind to three recommendation-specific signals—rare-positive value, low-diversity negative slates, and multi-objective reward resolution—a limitation we call the Static Boundary Bottleneck. We propose SAGE (Sequence-level Adaptive Gradient Evolution), which keeps the OneRec-style architecture and GBPO’s SFT-then-RLHF interface but replaces the static boundary with one slate-aware adaptive clipped surrogate: a sequence-level geometric-mean ratio sets the update to the generated slate, positive/negative adaptive bounds condition clipping on advantage sign and slate diversity, and a decouple-then-aggregate advantage preserves multi-objective resolution. Changing only the optimizer, OneRec-SAGE preserves top-K accuracy while improving offline cold-start recall by +89.9% to +101% and diversity by approximately +11% on Amazon, with consistent beyond-accuracy gains on RecIF-Bench—evidence that making the clipping boundary slate-aware, rather than changing the retrieval backbone, is the primary lever for rare-item exposure and list diversity on these offline proxies.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders are often trained with supervision first, then aligned to user feedback on whole slates with reinforcement learning. To keep training stable, each update may change the probability of generating a slate only by a fixed ratio set per sample, which smothers rare positive feedback on cold items and barely punishes repetitive negative slates. This Xiaohongshu paper proposes SAGE, which only changes the optimizer: ==positive slates get a higher cap on how far their probability can rise==. Repetitiveness is measured by the entropy of the slate's item categories, and the further a negative slate's entropy falls below its recent average, the further its probability may be pushed down. On Amazon data, top-K accuracy holds while offline cold-start recall rises by about 90% to 101% and diversity by about 11%.

papers.title: TGR-EvoDAG: A DAG-based Multi-Agent Code Evolution Framework for Generative Recommendation on Tencent
papers.authors: Junlin He, Junzhang Zhu, Yudong Li, Yihong Tang, Xuefeng Jiang, Wei Ma, Chengxiang Zhuo, Zang Li
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a dilemma: general-purpose frameworks lack domain-specific feedback, while recommender-specific frameworks rely on linear evolution. Crucially, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommendation (GR). Unlike end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded pipeline (tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm, existing evolution methods suffer from: i) cost blindness, squandering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-sighted evaluation, discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily regress metrics before downstream adaptation. To bridge these gaps, we propose TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework tailored for GR. TGR-EvoDAG models code evolution as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to maintain multiple evolution branches and merge complementary innovations, unifying advanced search with rich GR diagnostic feedback. We further introduce stage-aware cost planning to optimize GPU-hour budgets, and active downstream co-adaptation to navigate temporary regressions and unlock cross-stage gains. On public Amazon datasets, TGR-EvoDAG enables the first autonomous evolution of a complete GR pipeline, improving offline metrics by up to 37.4% and Agent4Rec simulated user satisfaction by 19.7% over the strongest baseline. Furthermore, in industrial deployment on Tencent's large-scale commercial media platform, the evolved GR achieves a 12.16% relative improvement in offline Hit@1 and a statistically significant 0.40% increase in online click-through rate (CTR).
papers.summary: Letting LLM agents rewrite code to search for better recommenders runs into two problems in generative recommendation. Retraining the tokenization, pretraining and alignment stages costs very different amounts, yet agents spend budget as if it were uniform. And a good upstream change often makes metrics worse until downstream stages adapt, so it gets discarded too early. This Tencent paper proposes TGR-EvoDAG, which ==keeps several improvement branches alive in a directed acyclic graph==. Each node is an edited version of the code that records which pipeline stages the edit touched and its retraining GPU hours. Upstream edits that first hurt metrics are kept until downstream edits adapt, then the branches are merged, and budget goes by expected gain versus retraining cost. On Tencent's commercial media platform, the evolved model raised online click-through rate by a statistically significant 0.40%.

papers.title: GUIDER: Generative User Interest Discovery via Explicit Reasoning with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jinke Wu, Yinghao Wu, Shuchang Liu, Yandong Bai, Qi Zhu
papers.abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven a paradigm shift in sequential recommendation from discriminative ranking to generative modeling. However, existing generative approaches predominantly rely on semantic IDs (SIDs)—discrete identifiers derived from hierarchical quantization that function as semantic black boxes. Solely designed for in-domain reconstruction, these opaque tokens preclude the mining of explicit user behavioral logic. In contrast, plain-text modeling unlocks the full inferential potential of LLMs, enabling superior generalization and precise, logic-driven interest discovery. To bridge this gap, we propose GUIDER (Generative User Interest Discovery & Explicit Reasoning), a framework that fundamentally decouples intent planning from item matching by reformulating sequential modeling within a rigorous closed-set semantic interest space. GUIDER first internalizes domain-specific semantics via continual pre-training and activates explicit reasoning through a hindsight-guided chain-of-thought strategy. Crucially, to ensure precise optimization of the generated interest set, we introduce Token-Adaptive Policy Optimization (TAPO). Addressing the credit assignment problem—where standard reinforcement learning indiscriminately assigns identical advantages to the entire response regardless of local correctness—TAPO employs a token-level advantage adaptation mechanism. This strategy explicitly differentiates valid interest circles from hallucinations by dynamically redistributing advantages based on fine-grained quality, while a dynamic thinking penalty suppresses redundant reasoning. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B testing on the Kuaishou platform validate that GUIDER not only achieves superior accuracy but also yields consistent gains in average app duration and effectively facilitates out-of-cocoon interest exploration.
papers.summary: The Semantic IDs common in generative recommendation are opaque strings of codes: it is hard to see what the model generated or why, and the LLM's own reasoning goes unused. GUIDER splits recommendation into two steps. ==The LLM first reasons in text about which interest circles the user may want next==. Circles are interest topics described in words and must come from a fixed set; items are then matched within the chosen topics. In reinforcement learning, invented circles outside the set lose reward, and so does overlong thinking. Large-scale online A/B tests on Kuaishou show steady gains in average app time and more exploration beyond users' existing interests.
